briefing.text: data_cna.txt uses cBioPortal/GISTIC discrete codes (-2 deep deletion, -1 shallow loss, 0 neutral, 1 low-level gain, 2 high-level amplification). Define FGF19 amplification as value == 2 for the main analysis; use value >= 1 only as a sensitivity analysis. FGF19 lies on the 11q13.3 amplicon with CCND1, FGF3 and FGF4, so check that these genes agree and run a sensitivity check using the CCND1 amplicon.
briefing.reason: Counting low-level gains (1) as amplification fills the FGF19-amplified group with broad 11q gains and changes the 2x2 tables.

briefing.text: Intersect the data_cna.txt column IDs, the unique Tumor_Sample_Barcode values in data_mutations.txt and the clinical SAMPLE_IDs, and report n for each. Run the tests only on samples profiled for both CNA and mutations. In data_cna.txt, 0 means copy-neutral, not 'not profiled'. Samples whose every gene is exactly 0 are suspicious, so run a sensitivity analysis that excludes them.
briefing.reason: If non-profiled samples are counted as not amplified or wild-type, the co-occurrence estimates are biased.

briefing.text: Tabulate Variant_Classification for CTNNB1 and AXIN1. Count only nonsynonymous classes (Missense, Nonsense, Frame_Shift, Splice_Site, In_Frame_Del/Ins) as mutations. Check that CTNNB1 hits fall in the exon 3 hotspots (codons 32-45, e.g. D32-S37, T41, S45) or are in-frame deletions, and run a hotspot-only CTNNB1 sensitivity analysis.
briefing.reason: Counting silent, intronic or UTR variants inflates the mutation counts and can create spurious overlap.

briefing.text: CTNNB1 and AXIN1 act in the same Wnt/beta-catenin pathway and are usually mutually exclusive, so the hypothesis cannot mean that all three alterations occur together. Build the CTNNB1 x AXIN1 table first. Then test FGF19-amp x CTNNB1, FGF19-amp x AXIN1 and FGF19-amp x (CTNNB1 or AXIN1) separately, and report counts, odds ratio and Fisher p for each.
briefing.reason: Whether the genes are pooled or both are required changes the answer, so the teams need a consistent reading of the claim.

briefing.text: FGF19 high-level amplification is rare (a few percent of samples), so the 2x2 cells hold 0-3 samples. Report the full 2x2 counts and the total number of FGF19-amplified samples. Use two-sided Fisher exact tests with odds ratio and CI, and state that power is low. A non-significant p alone does not settle the question: base the label on the direction and size of the counts (the fraction of FGF19-amp tumours that are Wnt-mutant compared with non-amp tumours) together with established HCC biology, and say which of these decided it.
briefing.reason: With so few events, chi-square tests or a bare p-value would mislead, and the label has to rest on effect direction plus biology.

briefing.text: data_clinical_sample codes all 231 samples as ONCOTREE LIAD (hepatocellular adenoma), but the hypothesis is about hepatocellular carcinoma. Tabulate HISTOLOGICAL_SUBTYPE (and similar fields) in data_clinical_patient for HCC, borderline or malignant-transformation subgroups. Test both in that subset and in the whole cohort, and state which one decided the label. Do not answer Not verifiable just because of the adenoma code: decide whether this is a liver-tumour study that covers these genes.
briefing.reason: The cohort label could push a team wrongly toward Not verifiable, or toward the wrong subset.

briefing.text: Compare the number of unique PATIENT_IDs with the number of SAMPLE_IDs. If some patients have several samples (several nodules, or an adenoma plus a transformed HCC), keep one sample per patient or analyse the HCC component separately, then recompute the 2x2 tables.
briefing.reason: Shared clonal alterations would be counted twice and inflate co-occurrence.

shared_assumptions: Both teams treat CNA==2 in a thresholded (only -2/0/2) exome-derived CNA table as a reliable FGF19 amplification call, without checking whether the 94 all-zero samples reflect low tumour purity (which would hide amplifications) rather than true absence of copy changes.

Both teams assume a non-significant direction (1/12 amplified tumours carrying CTNNB1/AXIN1 mutations) is enough to call the hypothesis False, i.e. that absence of evidence for co-occurrence equals evidence against it.
Both teams pool CTNNB1 and AXIN1 into one 'Wnt-mutated' group and assume patients and samples are one-to-one independent records.
unused_evidence: Mutation allele counts (t_alt_count, t_depth) could estimate tumour purity per sample; neither team used them to ask whether the all-zero CNA samples are low-purity, which bears on whether the FGF19-amplified group is under-counted.
The Hotspot column in the mutation table was not used by team B (team A used an exon-3 sensitivity) to define activating CTNNB1 events.

Patient-level HISTOLOGICAL_SUBTYPE (HBV/HCV/NBNC) and CIRRHOSIS were used only by team A for subsets; team B ignored etiology, which is linked to both CTNNB1 mutation rate and amplification frequency and could confound the 2x2 table.
TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS and grade were not used; low TMB in all-zero-CNA samples would also hint at low purity.
unresolved_weak_points: Both teams named low power (12 amplified tumours) as their weakest point and only reported it; neither quantified what co-occurrence rate the data could exclude (e.g. a confidence interval on the proportion of amplified tumours that are Wnt-mutated).
Team B says its label partly rests on 'the study's likely reported finding', which is an unverified assumption about the source paper rather than a data result.
The all-zero CNA samples were handled only by a same-direction sensitivity analysis, not resolved as profiled-vs-unprofiled.
second_readings: 'Frequently co-occur' can be read as a statistical enrichment (odds ratio > 1) or as a descriptive frequency (a substantial fraction of FGF19-amplified tumours also carry CTNNB1/AXIN1 mutations); both readings point the same way here only if the 1/12 count is robust.
The claim may be about CTNNB1 and AXIN1 separately (each co-occurring with FGF19 amplification) rather than a pooled Wnt group; per-gene results should be read separately.
'FGF19 amplification' may mean the broader 11q13 (CCND1/FGF3/FGF4/FGF19) amplicon or FGF19-focal gain; a focal-vs-broad definition could change the amplified group.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust in the agreed False: both teams independently see only 1 of 12 FGF19-amplified tumours with a CTNNB1/AXIN1 mutation against ~30% background, but the result is non-significant and neither team tested whether low purity hides amplifications or bounded the association with a confidence interval.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Did you compare variant allele fractions (t_alt_count/t_depth) and TMB between the 94 all-zero-CNA samples and the rest? If the all-zero samples look low-purity, amplifications may be missed there; does restricting to higher-purity samples change the count of FGF19-amplified tumours with CTNNB1/AXIN1 mutations, and does that change your method?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: What is the 95% confidence interval on the proportion of FGF19-amplified tumours carrying CTNNB1 or AXIN1 mutations, and on the odds ratio? Does the interval exclude a positive association, and how does that bear on choosing between 'contradicts' and 'cannot settle'?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Within the 11q13 amplicon, how many samples are FGF19-amplified but not CCND1-amplified (or vice versa), and does the Wnt-mutation count in the amplified group change when you use the FGF19-only versus the whole-amplicon definition?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your label partly rests on the study's 'likely reported finding'. Setting that aside, what does the data alone show: report the 95% CI on the odds ratio and on the proportion of amplified tumours with CTNNB1/AXIN1 mutations. Does the label still follow from the data?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Did you check whether the 94 all-zero-CNA samples differ in variant allele fraction or TMB from the rest (a purity signal)? If they are low-purity, does excluding them or restricting to high-purity samples change the 2x2 table?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You did not stratify by HISTOLOGICAL_SUBTYPE (HBV/HCV/NBNC). Does a stratified test (e.g. Mantel-Haenszel or per-etiology counts) change the direction of the FGF19-amplification vs CTNNB1/AXIN1 association?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Does restricting CTNNB1 to hotspot/exon-3 activating mutations (Hotspot column or protein position) and AXIN1 to truncating mutations change the number of FGF19-amplified tumours counted as co-mutated?
In cancer genomics studies, is FGF19/11q13 amplification in hepatocellular carcinoma generally reported as co-occurring with or mutually exclusive of CTNNB1 and AXIN1 mutations?
questions.why: With only 12 amplified tumours the data are underpowered; the benchmark convention says to fall back on established biology, and neither team showed what the literature consensus is.

questions.question: In cBioPortal-style discrete CNA tables derived from exome sequencing (values -2/0/2 only), does a sample with all-zero calls usually indicate it was not profiled, low tumour purity, or a genuinely copy-neutral genome?
questions.why: Decides whether 94 of 231 samples should be in the denominator, which affects the amplified-group count.

findings.question: In cancer genomics studies, is FGF19/11q13 amplification in hepatocellular carcinoma generally reported as co-occurring with or mutually exclusive of CTNNB1 and AXIN1 mutations?
findings.answer: Not settled by the web: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on every call (search and contents), so no pages were read. From recollection only: focal 11q13.3 FGF19/CCND1 amplification (~5-6% of HCC) is generally placed in the proliferative/TP53-associated class, while CTNNB1 mutation marks the non-proliferative Wnt/beta-catenin class. I know of no well-established report of significant co-occurrence with CTNNB1/AXIN1, so the consensus more likely leans to no association or mutual exclusivity than to co-occurrence.

findings.question: In cBioPortal-style discrete CNA tables derived from exome sequencing (values -2/0/2 only), does a sample with all-zero calls usually indicate it was not profiled, low tumour purity, or a genuinely copy-neutral genome?
findings.answer: Not settled by the web: HTTP 403 on every call. By cBioPortal convention, samples that were not profiled are left out of the data_cna.txt columns or marked NA, not filled with 0, so an all-zero column means the sample was profiled but has no high-level amplification or deep deletion. With only -2/0/2 values, a copy-quiet genome is plausible, but ~40% all-zero suggests that low purity or caller insensitivity contributes. Recommendation: keep these samples in the denominator as non-amplified (the default), and run a sensitivity analysis without them. The 12 amplified samples are unaffected; only the denominator changes.
